This Week in Virology hosts Vincent Racaniello, Alan Dove, and bat researcher Angela Mingarelli break down both papers in detail. The first, from Colin Carlson's group, analyzed 58,319 human outbreaks across 169 countries over a century and found that no single driver explains emerging infectious disease — instead, the strongest signal is that outbreak reports cluster near healthcare facilities, with odds falling a median 32% for each additional hour of travel time to a clinic. The finding is a detection bias, not a cause, and the hosts warn against misreading it as a reason to cut clinics. The second paper presents eight chromosome-scale Myotis bat genomes and finds that bat longevity and cancer resistance are likely byproducts of selection on antiviral immunity. The most striking result: bats adapt to DNA viruses through protein sequence changes and to RNA viruses through gene copy number changes — the opposite of humans. The paper centers on PKR, an antiviral protein that Myotis bats carry in up to three copies. The duplicated genes have persisted for tens of millions of years despite toxicity at high doses, suggesting bats have resolved a tradeoff that other mammals cannot easily manage. Mingarelli cautions that "bat is not equal to bat" — the eight species in the study are all North American, while the Old World species are the primary reservoirs for filoviruses and beta-coronaviruses. Key Elements Alan DoveAngela MingarelliVincent RacanielloMyotisPKRNatureColin CarlsonAnthony FauciMyotis lucifugusPeter SudmantDavid EnardTP53Rand PaulJeff Hawkins When you look at a map of outbreak reports, the United States, Canada, Russia, the Sahara, and Australia mostly appear blank. But that blank space isn't proof that disease doesn't happen there. It's proof of what happens when the nearest clinic is a day's drive away. A study published in Nature on 23 September 2026 analyzed 58,319 georeferenced human outbreaks across 169 countries from 1910 to 2022, spanning 32 different diseases. The goal was ambitious: identify which human-driven changes — deforestation, urbanization, climate shifts, livestock density — most reliably predict where new infectious diseases emerge. The answer, according to the paper's authors, is that no single answer exists. "The strongest and most surprising signal is that outbreak reports cluster near healthcare facilities," said Alan Dove, speaking on This Week in Virology alongside host Vincent Racaniello and bat researcher Angela Mingarelli of McGill University. Outbreak odds fall by a median of 32% for each additional hour of motorized travel time to the nearest clinic. Racaniello immediately flagged the dangerous interpretation. "That does not mean that if you close down the clinics, the outbreaks will go away." Dove finished the thought: "No, they will get worse. You just won't see them." The distinction matters. This is a statement about where outbreaks get recorded, not where they occur. Mingarelli called it the paper's most important contribution — she had not previously considered how much physical access to care distorts the public health record. The search for one big driver of outbreaks is failing The Carlson-led study, titled "The anthropogenic fingerprint on emerging infectious diseases," assembled outbreak records from bat viruses with epidemic potential, rodent-borne pathogens, mosquito-borne arboviruses, and zoonoses including melioidosis, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, and Plasmodium knowlesi malaria. For each outbreak location after 1980, the team extracted 16 covariates across five categories: detection processes, socioeconomic factors, ecosystem structure, land-use change intensity, and climate change. The statistical architecture was a Bayesian geospatial logistic regression with spatially structured random intercepts. Dove translated the jargon directly: the random intercepts are "a very fancy term for fudge factor" — a correction that absorbs regional variation the covariates can't explain. Mingarelli walked through why each component was necessary: logistic regression for the binary outbreak/no-outbreak outcome, Bayesian methods to express effects as probability distributions with uncertainty rather than single point estimates, and geospatial structure because "dengue in Vietnam correlates with dengue in Cambodia" — standard logistic regression wrongly assumes independence. The results defied tidy narratives, though one pattern held widely: outbreak risk was typically highest in mosaic landscapes, where people and livestock live alongside forests and fragmented ecosystems. Urban land cover was significant in 20 of 30 diseases tested, and healthcare proximity was significant in 15 of 23. Climate drying was strongly linked to outbreak risk for about a quarter of diseases. Forest loss, despite its popular reputation as the master driver of emergence, showed up in only a few systems. Finding Detail Outbreak records analyzed 58,319 unique outbreaks, 169 countries, 1910–2022 Diseases covered 32, including bat viruses, rodent-borne pathogens, arboviruses, melioidosis, CCHF, P. knowlesi malaria Highest-risk landscapes Mosaic landscapes where people and livestock live alongside forests and fragmented ecosystems Detection effect Outbreak odds decline a median 32% per additional hour of motorized travel to nearest healthcare facility (range across diseases: 1.2–96.7%) Urban land cover effect Significant in 20 of 30 diseases Healthcare proximity effect Significant in 15 of 23 diseases tested Climate drying effect Strongly linked to outbreak risk for about a quarter of diseases (8 of 31) Forest loss effect Found in only a few disease systems Racaniello pushed back on that last point. He immediately thought of the original Nipah virus outbreak in Malaysia, where bats displaced by deforestation ended up in pig farms, and Argentine hemorrhagic fever, tied to pampas converted to corn. Dove's response: "they're seeing those things, but they're not seeing them as the majority." Racaniello added that Nipah also involved an El Niño event on top of forest clearance — "it's never one thing." The paper's most consequential conclusion is negative: the results "do not support the idea that one-size-fits-all ecological interventions would be broadly protective against epidemic and pandemic threats." Diseases transmitted by arthropods to humans respond more strongly to ecosystem drivers and drying; directly transmitted zoonoses like Ebola and MERS show little evidence of shared drivers at all — possibly because the data are sparse, possibly because their ecologies differ fundamentally. Racaniello offered a concrete illustration of how the diagnostic gaps compound. In a DRC Ebola outbreak, patients who reached a clinic tested negative for the specific ebolavirus a test was designed for, were sent home, and infected their families. John Dye, who has field experience with Bundibugyo virus, told him early Ebola and Lassa overlap so much in symptoms they cannot be distinguished clinically. In a Lassa-endemic area, a negative Ebola test sends the patient home. Mingarelli raised a data question the paper doesn't answer: the maps show Canada, Russia, North Africa, Spain, and Portugal essentially blank, despite known outbreaks in those regions. "It's probably either a reporting problem or they didn't include those data." Myotis bats: 139 species, one genus, a 42-year lifespan in a body that fits in your hand The second paper, published in the same journal on 26 August 2026, turns from outbreak maps to bat genomes. Myotis is the largest bat genus — 139 species across six continents, emerging 33 million years ago. Within the genus, lifespan ranges sixfold: Myotis brandtii reaches 42 years, while the shortest-lived species makes it to seven. Those extremes diverged only 10.6 million years ago. "That is very, very abnormal," Mingarelli said. Bats break the standard rule that lifespan scales with body size. "You've got these little bats flying around living for 42 years. That doesn't fit the curve." The team, with co-first authors Juan Vazquez and Elise Lauterbur and co-corresponding authors including UC Berkeley's Peter Sudmant and David Enard, produced haplotype-resolved, chromosome-scale genome assemblies for eight Myotis species. Mingarelli said she had never seen a bat paper attempt haplotype-resolved assembly before, and called the results "some of the most contiguous mammalian assemblies" at nearly 99% complete, with 20,869 protein-coding genes. All eight species carry 44 chromosomes — remarkable across 33 million years of divergence — yet harbor six to eight thousand structural variants per genome relative to the group. PKR: the antiviral protein that bats duplicated — and learned to live with The functional centerpiece is PKR, or protein kinase R. It's an interferon-stimulated gene that senses double-stranded RNA produced during virus infection and shuts down protein synthesis. Racaniello explained why every virus on Earth cares about it: every virus genome carries some antagonist to PKR "because if you don't, you're out of business." Myotis species carry one, two, or three copies. PKR2 is the ancestral copy; PKR1 originated from a single duplication at the root of the genus; a third copy appears only in Myotis californicus. The duplicated and unduplicated haplotypes have been segregating for tens of millions of years. The team's functional work knocked out PKR in HeLa cells, then reintroduced one, two, or three bat PKR variants. The results were precise: PKR1 and PKR2 together produce an intermediate translation shutdown, with no synergy and no inhibition. PKR1 forms homodimers, but PKR1 plus PKR2 does not form heterodimers — the protein-protein interface has diverged. Both together restrict vesicular stomatitis virus and Sindbis virus to a similar extent as single copies. The effects are additive, not synergistic. Then the tradeoff: at high doses, PKR is toxic to cells. The authors suggest this toxicity may explain why duplication is rare in other mammals. Bats have apparently resolved it. How, exactly, remains unidentified. The genomic surprise: DNA viruses drive sequence change, RNA viruses drive copy number The paper's most striking finding came from a reference set of 5,527 manually curated virus-interacting proteins, or VIPs — host proteins with at least one experimentally verified physical interaction with a viral protein, RNA, or DNA. In Myotis bats, VIPs are enriched for positive selection. The enrichment strengthens when restricted to VIPs with experimental evidence of pro- or antiviral fitness effects. The pattern holds across 47 publicly available non-Myotis bat genomes. But split by virus type, the result is counterintuitive. Bat VIP adaptation is driven by selection on DNA-virus-interacting proteins — with no genome-wide enrichment for RNA-virus VIPs. In humans, the pattern is reversed: adaptation is driven by RNA VIPs. Other mammalian clades show a mix. Racaniello called the bat result "a big surprise." Mingarelli offered a hypothesis: Myotis are not reservoirs of the RNA viruses people associate with bats, so perhaps they carry more DNA viruses — "but we don't know." Dove distilled the two strategies into a memorable frame: "Maybe when you're adapting to DNA viruses, you need to change the protein and when you're adapting to RNA viruses, you just need more." The copy-number analysis confirmed the complementary pattern. VIP genes were more likely to have undergone expansions or contractions on at least one Myotis branch — and this was driven only by copy-number changes in RNA-virus VIPs. Bats adapt to DNA viruses through sequence changes and to RNA viruses through copy-number changes. Humans do the opposite. "Other mammalian orders show a mix of adaptation in both RNA and DNA VIPs," Dove said. "None show the absence of genomewide enrichment in RNA VIPs that they've just found in the myotis." Cancer resistance emerges as a byproduct The longevity analysis modeled body size and lifespan evolution across a supertree of a thousand mammals. Bats show some of the largest and most rapid lifespan changes among mammals, largely independent of body size. Bats experience a 40% greater increase in lifespan per 1% increase in body size than non-bat mammals. Myotis showed some of the fastest lifespan increases relative to their most recent ancestor. The cancer analysis found that 4%, 5.4%, and 20% of protein-coding genes — depending on the measure — have at least one region under positive or negative selection in cancer-related processes, enriched for immunity, cancer, and aging pathways. Among positively selected genes, most Nearctic Myotis lineages were enriched for cancer hallmark pathways, and the lineages with the greatest lifespan showed the strongest enrichment. Myotis lucifugus, the longest-lived, showed over-representation of DNA double-strand break repair pathways. The functional test applied neocarzinostatin, a radiomimetic agent that induces double-strand breaks, to fibroblast lines from four bat species. At low doses, M. lucifugus was the only species showing sensitivity after 24 hours — its cells died. At high doses, it showed the highest apoptosis and greatest viability drop of all bats tested. This matches the pattern seen in elephants, naked mole rats, and bowhead whales: longevity associated with increased clearance of damaged cells rather than repair. Mingarelli wished the study had included human or mouse cells in parallel: "it would be really nice to see compared to another mammal because I think it would be even more striking." The RNA-seq results filled in the mechanism. After 6 hours of neocarzinostatin treatment, cells upregulated cell cycle arrest and cell death genes while downregulating division, growth, and DNA repair pathways. At 18 hours, cell cycle downregulation continued and stress response genes came up. The strongest pathway enrichment in DNA-damaged cells was the innate immune response — and those differentially expressed genes were enriched among DNA-virus VIPs specifically. The authors' interpretation ties it all together: selection on the innate immune response may drive antagonistic pleiotropy in aging-associated traits. The antiviral adaptations that let bats tolerate viruses also gave them longevity and cancer resistance. Racaniello quoted the paper's conclusion: "Traits such as cancer risk, cellular homeostasis, and antiviral response have evolved in tandem due to pleiotropic selection at coinciding points in the evolutionary history of bats." Dove summarized the hypothesis: "bats have been assaulted with viruses. They've evolved. Evolution has provided them with strong innate immune systems. And at the same time, those also gave them longevity and anti-cancer properties." The paper frames the connection as a single chain, from viral pressure through immune adaptation to its two byproducts: Peto's paradox and the elephant model Mingarelli explained Peto's paradox: within species, cancer risk scales with body size and lifespan, but across species there's no correlation. Elephants carry 20 copies of TP53 — 40 alleles — versus one copy in humans. In vitro, elephant cells exposed to DNA damage undergo apoptosis significantly faster than human or other mammalian cells: they clear the cell rather than attempt repair. The energetic cost of that strategy in an elephant-sized body is enormous. Mingarelli questioned whether making a new cell is really cheaper than repairing one. Whales and naked mole rats use similar strategies. Mingarelli's central caveat runs through both discussions: "bat is not equal to bat" — a phrase her lab uses constantly. The eight species assembled in this study are all North American; the Old World bats — Rousettus, Hipposideros, Rhinolophus — are the primary reservoirs for the most lethal human pathogens, including filoviruses and beta-coronaviruses. What the Myotis findings mean for bat immunology broadly is unresolved. The species carrying the viruses that most worry humanity are the least studied. Dove added a caution of his own on cancer: "to be clear, death bats almost certainly do get cancer. We just haven't seen it yet. We don't want to start another one of those myths like sharks don't get cancer because sharks totally get cancer." Fauci, AI in classrooms, and the nitrogen cycle The episode also covered a listener question about the political persecution of Anthony Fauci, which Racaniello called "insane" and "purely for political purposes." Dove called Fauci "a national treasure" whose structural problem was that the NIAID director was never supposed to be the public voice of a pandemic — the CDC director and surgeon general "were just not on the job at that time." By speaking truthfully during the first Trump administration, Fauci made Trump look bad, and MAGA-aligned Republicans want him "tarred and feathered" for it. On AI in education, a listener cited Daniel Suskind's "teach both, test both" argument, with the calculator panic of the 1970s as the analogy. Racaniello noted his own classes use in-class exams specifically so students can't use AI on graded questions. And a long letter from a University of Illinois professor emeritus on the nitrogen cycle drew skepticism from both hosts on the feasibility of mass dietary change, though both acknowledged global population will decline sign…

Dove summarized the hypothesis: "bats have been assaulted with viruses. They've evolved. Evolution has provided them with strong innate immune systems. And at the same time, those also gave them longevity and anti-cancer properties." The paper frames the connection as a single chain, from viral pressure through immune adaptation to its two byproducts: Peto's paradox and the elephant model Mingarelli explained Peto's paradox: within species, cancer risk scales with body size and lifespan, but across species there's no correlation. Elephants carry 20 copies of TP53 — 40 alleles — versus one copy in humans. In vitro, elephant cells exposed to DNA damage undergo apoptosis significantly faster than human or other mammalian cells: they clear the cell rather than attempt repair. The energetic cost of that strategy in an elephant-sized body is enormous. Mingarelli questioned whether making a new cell is really cheaper than repairing one. Whales and naked mole rats use similar strategies. Mingarelli's central caveat runs through both discussions: "bat is not equal to bat" — a phrase her lab uses constantly. The eight species assembled in this study are all North American; the Old World bats — Rousettus, Hipposideros, Rhinolophus — are the primary reservoirs for the most lethal human pathogens, including filoviruses and beta-coronaviruses. What the Myotis findings mean for bat immunology broadly is unresolved. The species carrying the viruses that most worry humanity are the least studied. Dove added a caution of his own on cancer: "to be clear, death bats almost certainly do get cancer. We just haven't seen it yet. We don't want to start another one of those myths like sharks don't get cancer because sharks totally get cancer." Fauci, AI in classrooms, and the nitrogen cycle The episode also covered a listener question about the political persecution of Anthony Fauci, which Racaniello called "insane" and "purely for political purposes." Dove called Fauci "a national treasure" whose structural problem was that the NIAID director was never supposed to be the public voice of a pandemic — the CDC director and surgeon general "were just not on the job at that time." By speaking truthfully during the first Trump administration, Fauci made Trump look bad, and MAGA-aligned Republicans want him "tarred and feathered" for it. On AI in education, a listener cited Daniel Suskind's "teach both, test both" argument, with the calculator panic of the 1970s as the analogy. Racaniello noted his own classes use in-class exams specifically so students can't use AI on graded questions. And a long letter from a University of Illinois professor emeritus on the nitrogen cycle drew skepticism from both hosts on the feasibility of mass dietary change, though both acknowledged global population will decline sign...

analysis.brief_en: This news report discusses two studies that analyze the patterns of infectious disease outbreaks and the antiviral immunity mechanisms in bats. The first study, published in Nature, found that outbreak reports cluster near healthcare facilities, with a 32% decrease in odds for each additional hour of travel time to a clinic. This suggests a detection bias rather than a direct cause of disease occurrence. The second study examines how bats resist cancer and disease through antiviral proteins like PKR, which they carry in up to three copies. The research highlights the complexity of outbreak drivers, noting that no single factor reliably predicts disease emergence. The authors caution against misinterpreting the findings as a reason to reduce healthcare access, emphasizing that the results reflect where outbreaks are recorded, not where they occur. The study also raises questions about the completeness of public health data, particularly in regions with limited healthcare infrastructure.

Home Health & Wellness Thailand presents One Health approach and safe pork initiative at FAO conference Health & Wellness News Pattaya-Thailand Thailand Thailand presents One Health approach and safe pork initiative at FAO conference By Pattaya Mail October 4, 2026 0 1635 Share on Facebook Tweet on Twitter Dr. Saowapak Hinjoy presents Thailand’s One Health experience at FAO headquarters in Rome, highlighting community action to prevent infectious diseases. ROME, Italy – Dr. Saowapak Hinjoy, President of the PREZODE General Assembly, presented Thailand’s experience at the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). She advocated for integrating human, animal, and environmental data to support joint risk assessments and coordinated action plans to prevent infectious diseases at their source. At the same conference, FAO recognized Thailand’s “One Health for Safe Pork” initiative as a Good Practice and Innovation in One Health in Agrifood Systems. Since her election as President of the PREZODE General Assembly in December 2025, Dr. Saowapak, Senior Veterinary Expert at the Department of Disease Control of the Ministry of Public Health, has linked global collaboration with practical implementation in Thailand to prevent zoonotic and emerging infectious diseases through the One Health approach. Most recently, Dr. Saowapak served as a speaker and panelist at the FAO Global Conference for Actions on One Health in Agrifood Systems, held from 21 to 23 September 2026 at FAO Headquarters in Rome, Italy. During the session “Beyond Data: The One Health Decision Challenge in a Complex World,” she emphasized that sharing data alone is insufficient. Turning data into action requires all sectors to develop a shared understanding, set common priorities, and establish a joint action plan. Collaboration among PREZODE, PREACTS, and ASAMCO demonstrates a practical pathway from global frameworks to local action. PREZODE sets the overall direction for prevention, PREACTS translates the framework into implementation, and ASAMCO applies and tests the approach in local settings. During the “From Science to Action” session, Dr. Saowapak presented a case study from Nan Province in northern Thailand, where the risk of Streptococcus suis was assessed across the entire pork value chain, including farms, slaughterhouses, markets, food preparation, and consumers. The team translated the findings into community-level interventions and policies to improve slaughterhouse standards. The approach emphasized practical, safer alternatives and engaged young people to communicate health information through short, accessible videos for the public. Dr. Saowapak also contributed to discussions on strengthening the wildlife and environmental health workforce. She highlighted surveillance for Nipah virus, Plasmodium knowlesi, and Herpes B virus as examples of how wildlife and environmental data can help identify health risks before human cases occur. She proposed stronger links between FTP-WEBE, the public health Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), and FETPV for the animal health sector. During the conference, Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, the Department of Disease Control Foundation, and ASAMCO/PREZODE partners received FAO recognition for Good Practices and Innovations in One Health in Agrifood Systems for the “One Health for Safe Pork: A Community-Based Innovation to Prevent Streptococcus suis in a Hmong Village in Northern Thailand.” The initiative was implemented in Ban Nam Tuang, Mae Charim District, Nan Province. This achievement resulted from collaboration among public health and livestock authorities, hospitals, schools, local government organizations, community leaders, young people, and academic institutions. Representing the team, Dr. Saowapak received the FAO Certificate of Recognition on September 22, 2026. This recognition shows how One Health can begin with a real community health challenge and develop into practical, effective prevention measures by combining scientific evidence, cultural understanding, and meaningful local participation. PREZODE sets the overall direction for prevention, PREACTS translates the framework into implementation, and ASAMCO applies and tests the approach in local settings. During the “From Science to Action” session, Dr. Saowapak presented a case study from Nan Province in northern Thailand, where the risk of Streptococcus suis was assessed across the entire pork value chain, including farms, slaughterhouses, markets, food preparation, and consumers. The team translated the findings into community-level interventions and policies to improve slaughterhouse standards. The approach emphasized practical, safer alternatives and engaged young people to communicate health information through short, accessible videos for the public. Dr. Saowapak also contributed to discussions on strengthening the wildlife and environmental health workforce. She highlighted surveillance for Nipah virus, Plasmodium knowlesi, and Herpes B virus as examples of how wildlife and environmental data can help identify health risks before human cases occur. She proposed stronger links between FTP-WEBE, the public health Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP), and FETPV for the animal health sector. During the conference, Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, the Department of Disease Control Foundation, and ASAMCO/PREZODE partners received FAO recognition for Good Practices and Innovations in One Health in Agrifood Systems for the “One Health for Safe Pork: A Community-Based Innovation to Prevent Streptococcus suis in a Hmong Village in Northern Thailand.” The initiative was implemented in Ban Nam Tuang, Mae Charim District, Nan Province. This achievement resulted from collaboration among public health and livestock authorities, hospitals, schools, local government organizations, community leaders, young people, and academic institutions. Representing the team, Dr. Saowapak received the FAO Certificate of Recognition on September 22, 2026. This recognition shows how One Health can begin with a real community health challenge and develop into practical, effective prevention measures by combining scientific evidence, cultural understanding, and meaningful local participation.
